observation.visible_scene: A wide, low-angle view of a river or lake at sunset (or sunrise). The sun sits low and slightly right of center against a sky that grades from deep blue at the top to warm orange near the horizon, with a thin wispy cloud in the upper left. A dark, leafy tree/bush silhouettes the entire left edge; the far bank is a black silhouette carrying palm trees, slender light poles and small structures. A bright vertical sun-glitter column reflects on the water directly below the sun. The camera framing (tree, horizon, sun position) stays fixed throughout.
visible_changes: The water's sun-reflection column shimmers and changes length/shape from frame to frame (sometimes a long unbroken streak to the bottom edge, sometimes shorter or broken), consistent with surface ripples modulating a reflection rather than a moving object.

A small dark speck (most consistent with a bird in flight) first appears in the left-center sky around t=2.2 s (just left of the tall pole) and translates steadily rightward across the open sky, ending near the left rim of the sun by t=2.67 s; it is not present in the earlier frames.
No other object motion is detectable: the sun, tree, cloud, horizon structures and overall framing remain in the same positions, indicating a static camera and an otherwise still scene.
outside_clip_unknowns: The bird's entry point before it becomes visible and its path/destination after the last frame are outside the segment.
Whether the sun is rising or setting, and any longer-term change in its height, cannot be determined from this ~2.7 s excerpt.
The cause of the water ripples (wind, current, unseen disturbance) is not visible.
uncertain_details: The moving speck's identity (bird vs. insect vs. distant aircraft) and exact flight speed are inferred from a single small dark mark; only its rightward translation across the sky is supported.
Sub-pixel camera drift, if any, is below the resolution of the static background evidence, so the camera is treated as fixed.

Both ends are arbitrary crop boundaries, not the beginning and completion of an action. Motion
may already be underway in the first view and may continue beyond the last. The endpoints need
NOT match or connect as a loop. Do not judge different endpoints as a physical inconsistency,
and do not invent a trigger, contact, start, stop, landing, disappearance or completion to make
the excerpt form a complete story. Missing context outside this segment stays unknown.
If an editing cut is visible inside the segment, distinguish it from continuous physical motion;
do not invent a smooth transition or a causal mechanism to connect the two views.
Describe what is visible during the excerpt, the actual changes, and supported persistent
properties. Cover the main visible process, not just scenery. Distinguish object movement from
camera movement, reflection from separate objects, expansion from translation, deformation from
occlusion, and an already ongoing process from its onset. Only state what the clip supports;
do not invent causes, an earlier impact, an unseen operator, material identities or later outcomes.
Do not infer motion from one frame, a visible seam or a single pose. Static intervals are valid.
Do not supply named physics laws. Compare each important entity's first and last image positions
and their relative positions before describing motion. Treat camera motion as uncertain when the
background evidence is insufficient, and retain clear relative changes despite that uncertainty.
Return JSON {"visible_scene":"...", "visible_changes":["observation supported within the excerpt"],
"outside_clip_unknowns":["unseen prerequisites or outcomes, only when relevant"],
"uncertain_details":["..."]}. Be concrete and concise, in English. This is not a complete event reconstruction.
